senses.gloss:
jīvana
(‘living’)
------------------------------------------
Though the word means life in general, it is used as a technical term also.
See MANTRASAṀSKĀRA.

jīva
(‘individual सोउल्’)
------------------------------------------
Derived from the root-verb ‘jīv’ (‘having life’) the word ‘jīva’ means any living being. However, in the Indian philo-sophical systems the words जीव and jīvāt-man represent the individual सोउल् in bondage, subject to the cycle of transmigration.
There are differences among the various systems as regards the nature and number of the jīvas. If the advaita system considers the जीव as vibhu or all-pervading and ultimately identical with ब्रह्मन्, other systems consider it as aṇu or atomic in size, infinite in number and completely different from ब्रह्मन्.
In the state of bondage, the जीव has three śarīras or bodies (sthūlaśarīra or gross body, लिङ्ग or सूक्ष्मशरीर or subtle body and कारणशरीर or causal body), five kośas or sheaths (annamayakośa, प्राणमयकोश, मनोमयकोश, विज्ञान-mayakośa and आनन्दमयकोश) and also has three avasthās or states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् (jāgrat, स्वप्न and सुषुप्ति).
See also ĀTMAN.

jīvanmukti
(‘liberation [even] while living’)
------------------------------------------
The scriptures of Vedānta accept two types of मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् from transmigratory existence: जीवन्मुक्ति and videhamukti.
When a person attains आत्मज्ञान or direct experience of one’s true nature as the आत्मन् or the Self, he is liberated from future births. Hence he is a ‘mukta’. However, since the प्रारब्धकर्म that started the present body is still there, he continues to live, with all the experiences brought about by that कर्म. But his reactions to the experiences are now completely different since he has known from his mystic experience that he is the pure spirit and not the material body in which he has temporarily made his abode. Such a person is called a ‘jīvanmukta,’ one who is liberated even while living in the body.
When the प्रारब्धकर्म gets exhausted and the body falls, he attains ‘videhamukti’ (liberation from all bodies including the present one) which is like a river entering into an ocean and losing its identity.

Jīvagosvāmin
(d. A. D. 1609)
------------------------------------------
Among the prominent teachers of Bengal वैष्णविस्म्, जीवगोस्वामिन् has carved out for himself an important place. He was a nephew of the well-known Gosvāmins, Rūpa and Sanātana (disciples of Śrī कृष्ण चैतन्य) and lived the whole of his life at Vṛndāvan near मथुरा in Uttar Pradesh.
His works—which are prolific and belong to the अचिन्त्य-भेदाभेद स्छोओल् of वैष्णविस्म् are quite well-known. They are: Ṣaṭsandarbha (which includes a commentary on the Bhāgavata), Bhaktisiddhānta, Gopālacampū, Upadeśā-mṛta, Harināmāmṛta-vyākaraṇa and so on.
See ACINTYA-BHEDĀBHEDA SCHOOL.

Jīvanmuktiviveka
(‘a dissertation on जीवन्मुक्ति’)
------------------------------------------
This is a dissertation on the subject of जीवन्मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् even while living in the body, by the famous विद्यारण्य who was the founder of the Vijayanagara empire and a pontiff of the monastery at Śṛṅgerī (from A. D. 1377 to A. D. 1386). His place among the writers on Advaita Vedānta philosophy is very high.
This treatise is in prose and is spread over five chapters. The first chapter (Jīvanmuktipramāṇa-prakaraṇa) proves the reality of the जीवन्मुक्ति state by quoting profusely from many authoritative works like the Bhagavadgītā, the Mahā-bhārata, the Bhāgavata, the Laghuyoga-vāsiṣṭha and the Sūtasaṁhitā.
The second chapter (Vāsanākṣaya-prakaraṇa) deals with practical methods of overcoming and eliminating vāsanās or evil tendencies carried over from many lives, by suggesting appropriate remedies.
The third chapter (Manonāśa-prakaraṇa) deals in detail, with the subject of manonāśa or ‘(apparent) destruction of मिन्द्’ by drawing heavily from the Yoga-sūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.). ‘Manonāśa’ simply means the destruction of the tendency of the मिन्द् to rise by itself impelled by the old tendencies.
The next chapter (Svarūpasiddhi-prayojana-prakaraṇa) delineates five kinds of advantages that a jīvanmukta-योगि gets in life which includes great bliss.
The last chapter (Vidvatsaṁnyāsa-prakaraṇa) is a detailed commentary on the minor Upaniṣad, the Paramahaṁsopa-niṣad belonging to the Śukla Yajurveda. It gives practically all information connected with सṁन्यास including the code of conduct prescribed for a saṁnyāsin.
See also VIDYĀRAṆYA.

jīvat-śrāddha
(‘śrāddha [of oneself performed by] a person still living’)
------------------------------------------
Śrāddha (obsequial rite) is an ancient ritual. If a person does not have children or successors who are eligible to perform his śrāddha after his death, or, if he feels that none of them may do it properly, he may perform it himself for himself. This is called ‘jīvat-śrāddha’ or ‘jīvaśrāddha’. It has to be performed every month for a year and then every year for twelve years.
The procedure as described in some works like the Baudhāyana Gṛhyaśeṣa-sūtras (3.19) is quite exhaustive and complicated. Some of the steps involved in it are: ड़स्तिन्ग्, kindling the sacred fire and offering oblations with certain mantras from the Ṛgveda (4.58.3), giving gifts of prescribed objects, burning an effigy of his own. observing an अशौच (ceremonial impurity), performing एकोद्दिष्ट rite and a few other rituals.
See also ŚRĀDDHA.
